utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We will hear the testimony of the next witness today. Mr. Registrar, have we any information from VWS about protective measures being sought or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness didn't request any protective measures, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Then counsel has been assigned to the next witness in -- for reasons known to the parties. Counsel assigned is Ms. Tomanovic. You're there, Ms. Tomanovic. Welcome in this courtroom. You asked for a delay in the start today for one hour and that -- in view of the tight schedule and in view of the fact that we have a rather tight schedule today and tomorrow, the Chamber did not grant that request at this moment. Nevertheless, if you'd like to raise any matter, then I think it would best be raised in the presence of the witness. And I did understand that you would like to address the Court in private session. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and around the courtroom. It is correct. I would like to discuss an issue, and I would kindly ask for the witness's presence in the courtroom during that time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you'd like to address the Court in private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Since I have to mention a number of things that are best be kept in private session, at least for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the witness may be brought into the courtroom, and before he enters the courtroom, we should move in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now back in open session. May the witness be brought into the courtroom. Ms. Tomanovic, you had time to consult with your client?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the short period of 15 minutes, we have completed our consultations and the witness himself will tell you what his decision is. If you want me to, I can do that. But I think he would prefer to do that himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Decisions are on a question-by-question basis. Mr. Krajina, before you give testimony in this court, you're required to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Could I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Krajina. Mr. Krajina, before we start your examination, I will briefly set out your right not to incriminate yourself which you most likely have discussed in quite some detail now with Ms. Tomanovic. Under Rule 90(E), you are granted a right to object to making a statement which might tend to incriminate yourself. Now, what the Chamber then could do is whether or not to compel you seems, at this moment, not to be -- it seems that it's not necessary to deal with that at this very moment. If it comes to that and it perhaps may never come to that, then we'll further explain to you. That means that if a truthful answer of a question that will be put to you, if that may tend to incriminate yourself, that is, that you would give evidence which could be used against you and then, of course, more specifically now in the ongoing proceedings in Croatia, which might be prejudicial to your position, but it could be anything else. It's not limited to the prosecution. If we would ask you questions about other matters where a truthful answer would incriminate yourself, then, of course, the same would be true; but it is clearly understood that your thoughts are focussing on the ongoing proceedings in Croatia. So if an answer, a truthful answer, would be prejudicial for you, then you may object to answer that question. I will also briefly explain to you why that is. That is because in Croatia, as in most systems, you have no duty to give information which might prejudicial to yourself. Now, as a witness having given a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, of course, if you answer a question you would have to tell the truth, which could create a dilemma. The dilemma either not to tell the truth, and, in that way, protect your interests in the ongoing proceedings in Croatia; or to truthfully answer that question but then to jeopardise your own position in the Croatian proceedings. Now, that dilemma is a dilemma which should be avoided, and that's the background of this Rule. Therefore, I'll start asking you questions. If any question arises and if you are in doubt, you may consult with Ms. Tomanovic. If you are coming to an area where you consider that possibly a truthful answer would tend to incriminate yourself, then you may object. And if you want to consult with Ms. Tomanovic on that matter -- And, Ms. Tomanovic, I take it that it's perfectly clear to you that we are not -- your presence is not here to have an orchestrated testimony but that are you here for the primary purpose and that the witness may consult you for the reason that you advise him on whether or not it would be wise for him to decide to object to answer a certain question. Your role is clear. Your position is clear, Mr. Krajina. Any further questions in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's start. But before I put my first questions to you, you perhaps also should be aware, although it may not be of any influence to your decision, that, of course, this Chamber has received quite some evidence on the events in Grubori. Therefore, if it is a matter which would not -- is not risky for you, to say it that way, that you might give an answer that tends to incriminate yourself, that, of course, then this Chamber would establish facts without any additional knowledge you may -- additional knowledge of facts you could provide to the Chamber. So, therefore the fact that you would not testify on certain matters does not mean - just for your understanding - that this Chamber would then stay away from that as well. It's just your testimony which would then not be available. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's get started. Could I briefly address the parties. Is there anything I should have added in the present situation where the witness has consulted for at least some hours with the counsel, whether I should inform him in -- on any other aspect of his right not to incriminate himself? If not, we'll start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, Mr. Krajina, could you please state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Bozo Krajina, born on the 1st of January, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you state your -- could you state to what unit you belonged in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Anti-terrorist unit of Lucko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's a unit of the special police?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It is not a unit of the special police. It is an anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what rank you had in 1995? And I'm talking about August.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Specialist training instructor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, that Lucko Unit, could you tell us in what operations it was involved in the second half of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Operation Storm and Operation Storm Encirclement, or Ring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Operation Storm, from what moment to what moment?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Operation Storm, from the 4th to the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking you about the second half of August. So that is not in that time-period. Now --

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, that's not it. Operation Storm Encirclement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which took place when exactly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: On the 25th and the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The operations on the 25th and 26th had a specific name, Storm Encirclement?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the 25th, what was the type of operation the unit was conducting?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It was a search operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what area?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: In the area of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you involved in that operation on the 25th? Did you take part in it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in the morning of the 25th, were you briefed, and, if so, how were you briefed, that is, where and in what terms, about this operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, I don't really remember the morning and what the briefing was like, but I do know that there was some sort of conversation taking place with the operation commander and that the directions in which we were supposed to move and the areas we were supposed to search were defined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the operations commander was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Assistant Commander Josip Celic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were -- where had you stayed during the night of the 24th to the 25th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: In Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you remember whether you were briefed in Gracac, or were you briefed at -- after you had left Gracac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was no special briefing in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you then receive any direction as to how to move and from where to move?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this took place at the starting line, the point from where we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who took you there, to the starting line? Who knew where the starting line was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Assistant Commander Celic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how did you go there? By car, or by bus, or how many cars were there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: We used vehicles that were normally used by the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How many of you were there, approximately, on that day, as members of the unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Roughly 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you receive maps of the area?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, we received maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how was the unit organised that day? Did it operate as one unit, or was it divided in any way?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It was divided into groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many groups?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were they approximately equally composed in numbers?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you describe how, then, the groups were composed? What was the difference between the several groups?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: The groups differed only in terms of their numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were the groups led by specific persons? Were there group leaders?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. Each group had its leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the group leaders were?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Stjepan Zinic, Branko Balunovic, Franjo Drljo, and Bozo Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your group - and I do understand that you were one of the group leaders - what your group encountered and experienced during the operation on the 25th of August? You would like -- if you would like to consult with Ms. Tomanovic, then you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Switch off your microphones, if you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You object to answering that question. When I asked you that question, of course, I would have expected either this objection or a fully truthful answer. Is there anything you can tell us about that operation, even if it's not the complete story, so, therefore, leaving out any detail that could incriminate yourself. Is there anything else you could tell us about the operation? For example, when did it start; at what time approximately did it finish? I don't know whether that would incriminate you, but that might be a fact which -- I'm not suggesting anything. And please consult with Ms. Tomanovic, if -- if you have any doubts.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I consult with my client, I would like to let the Trial Chamber know the following: I don't know how privy you are with the statement the witness had given to the ICTY investigators, I would only like to recall the following situation: That any answer that my client may give today to a question about Grubori might result, and rightly so, in the cross-examination by any of the parties. Perhaps you might find it difficult to grasp why it is that he would not wish to answer a question, but answering a question might have a great -- grave consequences for him in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If any question in cross-examination, if any truthful answer to a question put to the witness in cross-examination would tend to incriminate himself, the same would apply. So, therefore, if I'm asking about the time -- I mean, the witness will be cross-examined anyhow on anything. Has -- well, the parties can cross-examine the witness anyhow. But, as I said before, this is mainly a matter of question by question. If I, therefore, ask about what time did it take and -- well, let's say the witness would say, From 4.00 to 6.00 in the afternoon, and if then, in cross-examination, one of the parties would say, Did you see any flames in Grubori, then even if he has answered the question in relation to the time, that he still can object to answer the question about the flames he may have seen in Grubori. So I don't know whether that's -- but I'm also looking at the parties, whether -- whether there's any dispute about what I just told the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from what consequences that would have for the evaluation of the evidence given by this witness. That -- that's, of course, a totally different matter. It may well be that if he answers some of the -- well, let's say -- some of the rather neutral questions and doesn't answer the other questions, then, of course, to what extent we could and should rely on the answers to the neutral questions, but that's another matter, as far as I'm concerned. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. And I do want to address that. Maybe -- I don't -- I wouldn't want the witness to be tainted by what I say, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we could ask him to -- Do you understand any English, Mr. Krajina? Do you speak or understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apart from that, legal English is even sometimes incomprehensible even if you do understand the language. Could you take your earphones off for a second. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the witness has stated earlier, when Your Honour asked the question about the events in Grubori and he deadlined to answer, I think if -- and I understand the Court's position about things like asking about the time or the weather -- I think what we're doing potentially is entering a slippery slope and eroding potentially the 90(H) privilege by getting into subject matter regarding that specific incident. I just think it's a fine line that perhaps -- I know the subject matter is obviously interesting and necessary for the Court to come to a resolution on what that particular incident, in terms of what happened there. But I think it is a very fine line to ask questions about when it started, when it ended. It -- potentially blending that -- I mean, if that -- if the witness feels that's self -- potentially self-incriminatory, the time that it happened or what kind of weather conditions there were, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I say the following. I could have imagined that the witness would have refused to answer the question, whether he was present during the day, whether he was a member of that unit. Now despite the fact that the Chamber received at least some evidence that he was, I could -- but once -- but even then, if for one reason or another, if you consider the time-frame to be self-incriminatory, for example, knowledge of these kind of things, and that's also the reason why I phrased the question very cautiously. I said is there anything you can tell us, without incriminating yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness can answer, No, I cannot, that comes down -- that would, as a matter of fact, repeat his objection to answering questions of this kind. At the same time, the Chamber and the parties have a duty do elicit from the witness what could reasonably elicit from him -- elicited from him as evidence, at the same time, fully respecting him, his right not to incriminate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do agree with Your Honour. And I do agree with the neutral methodology of the questioning. I don't have any problem with that. My concern is that this is an line. How close do you get to the line without crossing over it; that's really the concern that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what I just said is that the witness said, If I answer any question, I will be cross-examined on the events. Then I explained that if he thinks that he could answer a question without incriminating himself, that, if cross-examined on the events of the 25th, that we would take a similar cautious approach and that it's not, once given one answer because he has given one already, that, therefore, the whole of the 25th, that he would be compelled to answer questions. That seems to be based on a misunderstanding. Because it goes, as I said before, question by question. For example, you could cross-examine him on the make of the vehicles. And if you say we went there with our vehicles, then I -- I can imagine that the witness would have no difficulties in answering that. But if you would ask questions which are far more sensitive, then, of course, the same would apply and the witness would invoke his -- or would object to answering the question and we would, as you may know, unless it could not possibly be understood that a question could be self-incriminating, that we would respect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Totally understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just raising a sort of a caution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see you're talking about fine lines. It's the duty of this Chamber to carefully look at those lines and to draw them as sharply as possible and as cautiously as possible with full respect for the witness not to incriminate himself. Any further observations to be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just a comment, Mr. President. This is just as an officer of the court, since this doesn't involve our client, but there is some difficulty in the questions. I mean, I could just look at the question that you just gave right now about the vehicles and the makes of the vehicles and Your Honour noted that that wouldn't be necessarily culpatory. Well, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, that's right. That's the problem. In fact, it could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, therefore, Ms. Tomanovic is here. And if the witness has any doubt -- and as you may have noted, if Ms. -- if the witness has no doubt but if Ms. Tomanovic sees any problem there, I would not -- as a matter of fact, she --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- took the initiative also to communicate with the witness, and that's -- I didn't stop her to do that. So, therefore, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just complete my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, with regard to the neutrality of a question about the vehicles, it could be patently neutral. However, given the evidence that's in the Chamber, any response of that could be quite inculpatory unbeknownst to the witness or counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time it's the witness who invokes the right, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if he overlooks any possible [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's the problem, Judge. That's really, really -- with all due respect, Mr. President, that's really not something I believe we want to engage in, whether or not he overlooks something given those circumstances. Again, this has nothing do with my client. However, there is a difficulty when we get into those things about what is inculpatory. Number one we have the issue of whether or not this witness knows it's inculpatory, and the other is whether or not it's inculpatory unbeknownst to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that, well, let's -- let me not further comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you put on your earphones again. Yes. Is there anything you could tell us about the operation where, if specifically asked about that matter, you would not object to answer such a question? If you want to consult with Ms. Tomanovic, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I cannot answer any questions about that incident. Any answer to any such question would incriminate me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't ask about an incident, but I take it for granted that you refer to an incident which may have happened during this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where the Chamber, according to the Rule, may compel to you answer the question, the Chamber will not. Then I would like to move on. And perhaps we do it in broad terms. Is there anything you could tell us about the reporting, that is, to your hierarchical superiors, on these events? Yes, Ms. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I would have to consult with my client with regard to his answer to this particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please do so and feel free to do so even without the permission of the Court next time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I cannot answer any questions about reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you object to answering that question, as I understand. Whether you can or not answer is a different matter. But in court you say you fear that a truthful answer would incriminate yourself -- would tend to incriminate yourself and, therefore, you object to answering that question. The Chamber will not insist and will not compel you to answer that question. Now, let me -- would you give the same answer on not formal reporting but discussing the events with colleagues or anyone else, on what happened on the 25th? That -- would you also object to answer questions about informal conversations about the events?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: My answer would be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let me take you to the second day of what you called the Storm Encirclement Operation on the 25th and the 26th. On the 26th, was the -- the Lucko Unit, as you said, was involved in an operation. Could you tell us what that operation was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As for the 26th and what happened on that day, in the earlier morning hours, we were brought to the launch line, and our axis, as far as I can remember, was the village of Ramljane. And in Ramljane we were given our axis of deployment, and from the launch line we set out in groups, but we did not stay with the same groups all the time. As -- as the day progressed, the groups merged. We passed through the village of Ramljane. We did not stay there long. The whole area was uninhabited. We reached the final line of our operation. There were vehicles there, waiting for us to take us back to Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the group -- the groups merged. Did you start in a similar way as the day before, that is, in four groups; or were you already, at the start, divided in groups which were different from the 25th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: The groups were the same. And the manner of operation was the same, which means that we set out from the launch line, from the starting position. We spread out in a skirmish line, and we proceeded from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said later the group -- the groups merged. Do you remember where and when?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: That was during the operation, once we reached the village of Ramljane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was already in the village of Ramljane that the groups merged?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to state that for a fact. I -- I don't really remember whether it was in Ramljane or even before. But as far as I can remember, we merged in the village of Ramljane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In which direction did you move: east to west, west to east, north to south, south to north? Could you tell us approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I believe, and as far as I can remember, let me tell you, when are you in the field it's very difficult to determine the directions, and I believe that it was -- the axis was south-east/north-west. That was the axis of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this Chamber received evidence that east of Ramljane there is a road from Knin to Drnis, which is parallel to a railway track. Now, did you end at the railway track, or did you start at the railway track, or are you not aware of where that railway track and that road - I think the number is road 33 - is?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I only know that we ended our search at the railway station. That's the only thing that I remember, the only time I saw a railway line at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it assist you if we would have a look at map; or would you say, Well, a map wouldn't help me in further refreshing my memory as to in what direction we moved?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I'm sure that it would help me to remember the direction of movement. If -- if I were to look at a map, that would certainly help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am -- I think it's P190, which is the large map, which we could zoom in then on the relevant area as we did before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have P190 on the screen. It takes a while to get a map on -- could we zoom in Knin-Drnis area. Yes, perhaps that's ... yes. Could we further zoom in. A little bit -- the northern part of the -- not -- not further to the south. Further to further north. By far, further north. Could we -- no, we should ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we zoom it a bit further. Yes. Witness, this map is the Ramljane -- is about the Ramljane area. Do you see the north/south main road approximately in the middle of the map?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see, in the upper part, the name of a village Dobrici?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you see Vujakovici to the west of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see further to the west a small settlement by the name of Perica tor?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this map assist you in telling us in what direction you moved?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Looking at the map, and starting from Perica Tor towards Dobrici, and if that was that, then the direction of our movement would be from west to east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you describe what your group encountered and experienced during this operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: What I remember from that day and from that operation is this: I saw Commander Stjepan Zinic in the village. The village was abandoned. There was nobody in the village. We did not stay there at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... interrupt you for a moment. You said "in the village." What village are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Ramljane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue. You saw Mr. Zinic there.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: We left the village and we proceeded. We continued our operation. In one part of our route we reached a facility. In the courtyard of that facility there was some ten individuals. I remember that one person from the column went in the direction of those individuals and the intention was to ask them whether we were on a good route. We proceeded. We did not see anybody else. And on that second day, operation ended at the Strmica railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you say we ended at the Strmica railway station, did you walk to the Strmica railway station? Is that -- you reached that by walking?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. We went there, and we reached that on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, perhaps Ms. Tomanovic carefully listens to my next question. This Chamber has heard evidence that the operation on the 25th ended at a railway track close to the Strmica railway station and that it was in that area that the unit would find their vehicles again, boarded those vehicles, and returned to Gracac. Is there any way that -- any chance that you're mixing up what happened on the 25th and the 26th? Because it's quite a distance to walk to Strmica from this place.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that I have made a mistake, that I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then take you back to the operation. You said you saw some ten people. You asked whether you were on the right route. Did you see any smoke or fire at -- no, let me first ask you. Was there any exchange of fire, of fire-arms, during that operation on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, there was no exchange of -- of fire at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't hear any fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, I did not hear any fire being opened. What we heard were just sporadic shot, as we called it, an individual round being fired every now and then. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you use any anti-tank weapons on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: On that day, our mission was to scour the terrain, and when that was the mission, we did not carry any anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see any smoke or any fire on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, we -- we could see smoke. As we were leaving the village, as we -- as we were at a certain distance from the village, we could see smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see any fire? Any burning structures?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I did not see fire, but we could see smoke. As I've told you, we were at a certain distance from the village. As we were leaving the village and as we were at a certain distance from the village, we could see smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that you reported on the events on the 26th? I should say "whether you reported."

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, I did not write any reports about the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have P771 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you able to read it, Mr. Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, I can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this --

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: But it would be even better if the whole thing could be blown up a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd like to have it on the -- on the entire screen, perhaps, I think everyone who needs to consult the English text has it available.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina. The -- my first question was whether you could read it. You've answered that question. My second question would be: Do you recognise this as your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I don't recognise this. And I claim that this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the first time that you see this report, Mr. Krajina. You --

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. I've never seen this report before. This is the first time I see it, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say this is not what I wrote, you did not write the report, and this is not your handwriting. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is my testimony. I did not write this report. This is not my handwriting, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we don't have to pay further attention to what is written -- well, this report says, even if it's not your report, that: "As a result of the use of anti-tank weapons, some buildings caught fire and that in the vicinity of those buildings there were stacks of hay and straw." Does that report, even if it's not yours - and we have other reports from that day; I'm not intending to read all of them to you - does that in any way refresh your memory in relation to your earlier answers?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It does not tell me anything new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you earlier said that you had no anti-tank weapons, that you have seen smoke, but you have not linked in any way the use of anti-tank weapons to fire and smoke. So, to that extent, it is new, comparing this report with your early -- your testimony earlier today. So I just wanted to put that to you as an addition to whether this refreshes your memory.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, it does not refresh my memory. I've already said before that, as far as I remember, no anti-tank assets were used. That would have been obvious had that been the case. And as for the rest, there's nothing in it that could refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also not, because that seems to be new here as well, that the unit was pursuing parts of the terrorist group that was on the run and that you came -- you had come under infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: On the 26th, there was no such contact, as the one you hint at in your question. There were no terrorists, anti-tank weapons were not used. On that second day, we simply passed through the village without stopping there. At a certain point, we met a number of individuals and proceeded on our way. I don't remember anything related to the use of anti-tank weapons. Well, not that I don't remember. Probably had there been such fire, I would have remembered it. The use of anti-tank weapons is not something that could be overlooked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were talking, you passed through the village. Would that be true that -- did you pass through other villages as well; or was it just the Ramljane village; or whether there were any other settlements that you passed through?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As I said, we passed along the road and through the village. I only remember that one house where there were a number of individuals present. And I can't really tell you that we passed by abandoned houses on our way. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because this report mentions a village of Grkanici, whereas when you are talking about the village, I understood that you were talking about the village of Ramljane.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I have a vague memory of Ramljane. Now, as for Grkanici, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, on the map at some -- at some -- and in other evidence this Chamber has received, a village of Vujakovici was mentioned. Do you have any recollection of that village?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I don't recall that village either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Vucenovici. Does that ...

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that you passed only through the village of Ramljane or whether you also passed through other settlements, small groups of houses?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As I've already said, I do recollect the village or hamlet we went through. I don't remember the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you nowhere encountered any terrorists, or you were nowhere shot at by infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No. We never came across terrorists and -- or under fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it's -- we need a break first. We'll resume at 20 minutes past 11.00. Ms. Tomanovic, if you would need further time, then it -- perhaps it could be arranged that you further discuss matters with Mr. Krajina. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. I already inform the parties, but I think you are informed about it already, that we'd like to continue in the afternoon. Our expectation at this moment would be, but we still have to find out how reliable that is, that we might finish in one session this afternoon. And because, then, for the second half of the afternoon, we have -- another case is scheduled in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina, we left off after I had asked you some questions about the events and the handwritten report on the events of the 26th of August in the Ramljane area. Now, during or after that operation, do you -- do you have any recollection as to having seen Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As the operation concluded and we got into our vehicles, we set off for Gracac. At one stretch of the road, and I can't tell you which, we came upon Mr. Markac, who stopped our column, and that's where conversations took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you -- got off your vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, we got out of our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now was the whole unit assembled there or was it just some members of the unit which were part of a conversation with Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: The whole unit gathered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there anyone in the unit which would not have heard what Mr. Markac said? Of course, you can't tell us whether someone heard or not, but was there anyone at a distance from Mr. Markac that you assessed that he could not hear what Mr. Markac had said?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us, what did Mr. Markac say?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: He roughly said that we should not have done that, and that, for several reasons, somebody sent word that we should all be arrested and shipped to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it planned that you would be shipped to Zagreb anyhow, or was that something new for you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: There were no specific plans in place. The plan was that, once the terrain was searched, we would head for Zagreb. But there were no special plans made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, he said, you shouldn't have done?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you now how it was that he said it, but he probably meant the burning of houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "he probably meant." Was he referring to the burning of houses? I mean, if someone says you should be arrested, I'd like to know what I should be arrested for, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: You see, the conversation took place by the road, on our way back. Groups of people got out of their cars. And since these individuals were young people, 19-year-olds not that trained in what they were doing, it was customary for us to be at the rear of the column. So by the time I got out of my vehicle, discussions were already taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any response from members of the team to what Mr. Markac said?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge and based on what I heard, he had an argument with one of the leaders of the groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Franjo Drljo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said based on what you heard. You mean you personally observed, you heard when that argument was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. While I was there, I was listening to that part of their conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What did Mr. Drljo say?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how precise I can be in trying to quote their words. I think it was roughly the following: What was it that I did? Well, I can't really repeat the words because I don't remember them. But I think the gist of what they said -- what he said is something I conveyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then repeat that, because then I may have missed it. What was the gist of what Mr. Drljo said, in response to Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, I said the gist was, I did it, so what can you do about it? What can you do to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you had not seen any smoke or fire up till the moment that you arrived at the finish line. Now, didn't you say, We didn't do anything; or -- I mean, you told us that at least your unit had not seen any smoke that early or had not seen any fire that early.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to follow all this, what I said was that, on our way out of the village and as we were at a certain distance from the village, smoke could already be seen. What I said we didn't see was fire, flames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you said that; I just verified. So -- and you linked the words of Mr. Markac with the smoke you had seen which you considered possibly the result of burning structures. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. You can understand in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did any of the other team members respond to what Mr. Markac said?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it during that conversation that reporting, writing reports, was, at any moment, mentioned by whomever, by ...

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: At that point, there was no mention of writing any reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever a moment that you were instructed to write a report on the events of the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, instructions, not really; but some indications could be told, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that, simply because I don't know. Given my previous membership of the unit, where I did not have occasion to write reports, and when I tell you that indications were given, well, we would give some indications to the effect of how much ammunition was spent. And that's what I meant when I said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, "indications," is that a kind of a rough oral reporting you are referring to, or putting it on paper, or ...

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. I meant orally and giving an approximation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as the Ramljane operation is concerned, do you remember to have ever been invited or that it was ever suggested to you that you write a report about the events on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I wasn't asked to write a report, nor was anyone else, and I never wrote a report about Ramljane and the second day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina, this Chamber has heard evidence and has seen other reports similar to the one I showed you earlier, which were written by the other team leaders. And the Chamber also received evidence that they were specifically invited to write such reports. So, therefore, you would be the only one who was not invited and did not write a report on the events; I'm talking about the 26th, Ramljane. I'm just seeking your comment on why you were in a different position compared to the other group leaders.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I cannot account for the fact that somebody else wrote a report. I cannot give you an explanation for it. But I definitely do not recollect writing a report about the second day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to move on and ... after the encounter with Mr. Markac, where did the unit go? Did you go back to Gracac, or did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: We set out for Zagreb and did not stop in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You returned immediately to Zagreb. Was that for the whole of the unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. The entire unit set out for Zagreb right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't have any personal belongings that were left in Gracac which you had to collect?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Given the number of vehicles involved, given the operations involved, and orders that came from the top, we always used vehicles. We carried everything in our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we earlier did talk, or, rather, did not talk much about the events on the 25th in Grubori. Did you, at any other time - so I'm not talking about the 25th, I'm not talking about the 26th - but did you at any other time ever return to Grubori or the near vicinity of that village? I don't know whether you have been there, because we didn't discuss it. But did you ever go there, well, let's say 27th, 28th, any day after the 25th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, never after those events did I go to the area, let alone visit any of these villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the next issue I would like to ask you questions about is about reports that have been written about the events in the Plavno area, including Grubori, on the 25th. So this clearly now relates to the Grubori event. The Chamber has received in evidence reports, written reports, about what happened on the 25th. My first question to you would be: Whether you ever wrote a report on the events of the 25th? And I'm not surprised that Ms. Tomanovic wants to consult with you, or that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the entire question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether you ever wrote a report on the events of the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You object to answering that question. Are you aware of any of the other group leaders writing reports on the events of the 25th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you ever instructed or invited to write a report, irrespective of whether you did so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you ever seen a report which bears your name and is about the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will move on to another subject. Did you, after the operation and then the years following, did you ever hear any information as to who would have been responsible for the death of persons whose dead bodies had been found in Grubori on the 25th of August or in the days immediately following that 25th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: By your leave, I would like to explain the situation I was in at the time more extensively, and then you will conclude for yourself what the answer is. Following all these events, before which I had gone through a personal tragedy involving my family, I spent a little time in the army in early 1996 -- or, rather, I spent some time in the army because of my speciality which is explosives. After having talked to Mr. Markac, he decided to deploy me to various parts of Croatia in order to be engaged in mine clearance activities. Now, why did I make this introduction? For several months until early 1996, I was in the unit; whereas, from 1996 up until late 1999 or early 2000, I only went to be together with the unit sporadically and did not have occasion to meet the members of the unit that often which prevented me from discussing any sort of events with them. I don't know if I've made myself clear enough or sensible in all of this. But I wanted to portray the situation I was in, i.e., I did not have many contacts with members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's not really an answer to my question. My question is whether you heard anything about perpetratorship of incidents that may have taken place in Grubori. Whether it was in 1995, in 2000, in 2005, yesterday, whatever.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. I don't know who may have done it. I never spoke to anybody about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in an interview which took place in 2005, you are reported to have said that, at that time, you had recently heard stories but that you'd rather not repeat the stories. Does that, in any way, refresh your recollection as to whether you ever heard any stories about this?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember ever having stated that I'd heard stories. But it is possible that I did not want to go over some stories. But I didn't say anything specific. I don't think it's very mature or responsible to tell anybody what you heard, what rumours have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you are asked about that, it's for the Chamber who receives that evidence to see what the probative value of it is. So, therefore, my question again: "In 2005 - and with -- if I'm misrepresenting that evidence, I'll hear from the parties. I'd rather not go through the whole exercise of going through it. In 2005, you stated that you recently had heard such stories, that you would rather not repeat the stories also because they might turn out not to be true. And that everyone in the Lucko Unit knows the stories, and that Mr. Janic knows that story. And that's in a recorded interview. Does this refresh your recollection as to what you said in 2005, which is five years ago?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I remember that interview. I remember who the interview was with. And I remember that a question was worded to that effect. I don't remember, as I sit here today, what I said. I -- the interview took two days with certain people, and over those two days, I believe that I may have said something to that effect. But, as far as I can remember this particular question, and now you have jogged my memory, the question was, If I didn't know anything about those stories, is there anybody else who would be privy to any of the rumours. And I didn't only mention Janic but I also mentioned Ranko Ostojic, if my memory serves me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you tell us what those rumours were?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I did not mention having heard any stories myself. What happened was this: They asked me if I was able to tell them if there was anybody better suited to know what stories were told among the men. And then I mentioned those two names. I really don't remember having said anything specifically about any stories that I may have heard. And the way you put it now is it seems that I did hear stories but I never conveyed those stories, I didn't want to convey any of the stories that I might have heard, but I -- I, rather, pointed a finger at somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you're invited - and I'm asking you - to convey the stories to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I emphasise once again: I don't remember that I used a single word that would indicate that I was aware of the contents of any stories or any stories at all. And I really don't know what you expect me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you say, I don't want to tell the story because they may be not true, then it comes as a surprise that you say, I don't know the stories. Because then you would have answered that question, I can't tell you the stories, because I don't know what they are. That's different from saying, I don't want to tell the stories. And if you say that everyone else knows the stories, then, at least, that also suggests that you are aware of the content of stories, rumours, whatever you call it. And we could check that, but I don't have the 65 ter number of the 11th of January, 2005, interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's 7550, Mr. President. And if you could tell me the page number on the e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are at part 2 - I have split that up - part 2, which starts at 128 and continues until 132 and 133. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we ask the witness to take his headphones off, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take your earphones off for a second, Mr. Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the risk of being provocative, I object to this line of questioning because this -- what you're asking this witness to do is to speculate upon speculation. And the -- whatever value - the witness has already twice said he doesn't know of any stories - but whatever value these stories might have is miniscule. And there is -- the only probative value is that the Bench is cross-examining this witness on his credibility with respect to what he said about stories in his testimony and what he said about his stories in his statement. And I would like to further state on the record that what he said on his statement about the issue of the confrontation of Mr. Drljo was quite different from what he said in court and the Court -- what he said here in court, and the Chamber did not vigorously cross-examine him on the discrepancy there. So it's my position that with this particular line of questioning, you're asking, first of all, the witness to speculate; and second of all, I believe that picking and choosing the issue on which the Chamber wants to test the witness's credibility on is dramatically unfair to my client in this circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, first of all, if there is any area where you would find it appropriate to further test the credibility and the reliability, of course, you have an opportunity do so. To say that the Chamber is under a duty to test, in every respect, if it, at all, puts the reliability and the credibility to a test, that it's under a duty to do that with every inconsistency, I would like to hear any authority of such a duty for the Chamber. Secondly, I do not invite the witness to speculate. I just ask him what the rumours were that he heard or what the stories were that he heard. Nothing else. Nothing more. Nothing less. I'm not asking him to invent stories, just where, at an earlier occasion, he told about stories, and where he said, I do not want to give the stories. The witness now says -- well, at least -- you could consider his answers that they have some evasive element, and what I'm doing is, at this moment, to further test his evidence. But, again, to say, If you touch upon one element of inconsistency, if you are testing the credibility and reliability in this respect, that the Chamber has a duty to test that in every respect, that's not a duty for the Chamber, as it is not a duty for the parties. Or are you aware of any practice in which you say, Once you start testing the reliability and the credibility of a witness, then have you to do that on every possible issue where you could reasonably do so. That's apparently what you require of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you can cross-examine the witness on his credibility and reliability on the matter you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I never said it was a duty, Your Honour. I said it was [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said it was unfair to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do believe it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the Chamber is under a duty not to behave unfairly to your client. So, therefore, it's -- I -- with this rather strong words that it's unfair to your client, since I understand that a Chamber should not behave unfairly to one of the accused, it comes down to the same as having a duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's my position, Your Honour, and I wanted to put it on the record, that I'm here to protect the interests of my client. It's my position that the manner in which the Chamber is testing the credibility of this witness, specifically with this issue, as compared to the issue of the confrontation, is not fair to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record. I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you put your earphones on again, Mr. Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, after having consulted my colleagues, could you tell us what those stories or rumours were, if -- no, let's me -- could you tell us what they were. And perhaps I take you back to your statement. Could we go to -- it's page 133, but I don't know whether that's also the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this is 133 of section 2, that will be on e-court page 296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 296. Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, you are recorded to have said the following. You first said: "It's difficult for me to say something that could be following me or haunting me for my whole life." Then you further said: "You see, I said I know about the story, I can't say I have the information." And then you say: "Let's say I tell you the story and it turns out the story is not correct at all." Now, all those answers - and we could go through more of the pages - do suggest that you know what the stories are but that you are hesitant to convey them to the person who interviews you. Now, my question to you is again: Could you tell us what that story or those stories were?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I can see that one could conclude that I did know the stories from the answers that you have just read out to me. But let me tell you once again, whether you believe it or not, I am not aware of the contents of any of the stories. The only story that continued to be told was that somebody will be taken to task, will be held responsible for the events that had happened. To this very day, I don't know, I'm not aware of any stories, although contrary -- the contrary may be concluded from my answers, but I still adhere by my statement that I never as much as hinted that I was aware of the contents of the stories. However, when I was asked whether there was somebody else who would be privy to the contents of those stories, since I didn't know any of them, and the two persons that I named were at the very top, or close to the top, I mentioned the two of them. That's the only explanation of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina, I have no further questions for you. Could I receive an estimate of the times needed for cross-examination. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, less than a session. I believe about, you know, half to two-thirds of a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. About the same, probably less than -- half to two-thirds of a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Two times a half is a whole session. Two times two-thirds is one session and a half. Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the clock. There's a fair chance that -- we need another break. There's a fair chance that we would not finish before the lunch break. We'll certainly finish in the first session after the lunch break, but depending on your efficiency, you may be in a position to save yourself a -- an afternoon session. Because, after the break, we'll have five-quarters of an hour left. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Perhaps when I said you could save yourself an afternoon session I was a bit too quick because we have some housekeeping matters which I had on my mind to deal with a after we had finished with this witness. So if we finish before the lunch break then there still would be an afternoon session. But, on practical matters and whether the accused wanted to be present at that moment, of course, is a different matter. That's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krajina.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will start off by asking questions that don't relate to the substance of the events in Grubori so that you won't find any difficulty in answering the questions. To start off with, is it correct that you were promoted as an assistant commander within the Lucko Unit in November 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you promoted after Operation Storm? Maybe the time-frame was incorrect. But were you promoted as an assistant commander of the Lucko Unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: I was promoted into instructor of specialist training which is one level below, and that was after Operation Flash. Or, rather, between Operations Flash and Storm. That's when I received that decision to be promoted as an inspector [as interpreted] of specialist training. In other words, even before Operation Storm, I was an instructor. Before Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will have to correct the transcript. I believe that it will be of assistance to the Prosecutor. Mr. Krajina said on page 47, line 17, not an "inspector" but an "instructor."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instructor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there is a major difference there. Not an inspector but an instructor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina, were you promoted after Operation Storm, any time after Operation Storm, to a position above what you held during the course of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: In 1996, yes. That's when I was promoted as an assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's just what I wanted to establish. Now, prior to setting off on operation -- on the search operation on 25th or on the 26th, did you receive any instructions from either Mr. Celic or any one of the members of the inner control branch or any other commanders or Mr. Markac as to how to treat civilians or prisoners, when you took them, or how to treat private property?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Since we had been trained during our regular training, we already knew and were informed about certain conventions. During our regular training, we had learnt about that, and during previous operations, that was normal. And I repeat: During our training, we had learnt about that. And as I sit here today I really don't recall that anything special was said about the Rules of International Law on the eve of that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Krajina, the Chamber questioned you about reports, and now I'm moving to the operation on 26th August, that is, the operation conducted in the area of Ramljane, and you were questioned about reporting after the incident. My first question is: Do group leaders submit written reports after search operations, generally?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: When it comes to a general question, I can answer that it is only normal that group leaders do submit reports. But in a certain way, and with a bit of -- of -- but not with a delay. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, but my question is do group leaders submit written reports? Not oral reports, but written reports? I'm referring to special instructors leading groups in the terrain. Do you submit reports to the assistant commander who is leading the operation on the -- the -- the activities of the day on the particular operation, as to what your group went through? Do you understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Yes. They submit written reports and only written reports. And at least that was common practice at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say "they," you're including yourself? You submit written reports after an operation; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: Could I please consult with my counsel? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to understand my question, Mr. Krajina? My -- my question is: You, as a group leader, leading a group in an operation, at the end of the operation, do you submit a written report about the activities of your group? Let's say in the -- generally, if it's Mr. Celic who is commanding the operation, to Mr. Celic, or if it's -- if the operation is commanded by somebody else, to that person?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: In general terms, or generally speaking and speaking from practice, it was only the commander of the entire operation who submitted a -- reports. I don't know if I made myself clear enough. Did I answer your question properly? In general terms, as far as I know from previous practice, and given the fact that I was not at those levels, I cannot speculate whether that was a rule or not. I can only speak in general terms. At the moment when I was promoted to a certain level, the common practice was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krajina, I think you misunderstood me. You know, as I understood, you were a special instructor leading a group in the course of 26th August operation. Now, in such instances, you as a group leader - I'm not asking about the assistant commanders, the commanders who lead the entire operation - the group leaders, are you required -- as I understand your testimony, what you just said, you are not required to submit written reports. It's only the commander who leads the entire operation that submits written reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: In this particular case, or in such cases, the common practice was that group leaders, leading certain groups, also submitted written reports. But since there were hints that certain events might have happened, then group leaders were asked to submit reports. And if nothing has occurred during an operation, if there were no unusual things happening, then it was only the commander of the entire operation who submitted his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, today when the Chamber, His Honour, asked you about a report on the 26th, this is what you said. You -- this is at page 34: "Was it during" -- No, it's -- you were asked a question: "Was it during that conversation that reporting, writing reports, was, at any moment, mentioned by whomever ..." "At that point, there was no mention of writing any reports." Then you were asked a question: "Was there ever a moment that you were instructed to write a report on the events of the 26th of August?" This is the question that the Judge asked you. And your answer was: "Well, instructions, not really; but some indications could be told, yes." "When was that?" "I wouldn't be able to tell you ... simply because I don't know. Given my previous membership of the unit, where I did not have occasion to write reports, and when I tell you that indications were given, well, we would give some indications to the effect of how much ammunition was spent. And that's what I mean when I said it." Wait a minute, Mr. Krajina, please. Then you go on to say, you were asked questions: "Now, as far as the Ramljane operation is concerned, do you remember to have ever been invited or that it was ever suggested to you that you write a report about the events on that day?" "I wasn't asked to write a report, nor was anyone else, and I never wrote a report about Ramljane and the second day." Now, after the operation on Ramljane, did you provide a verbal report to Mr. Celic as to the fact that nothing happened in the course of the operation with regard to your group? Did you provide a verbal report?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, my group was not that important in the whole matter. And I don't recall talking to Celic about any events.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you clearly said -- your testimony here was that in the course of this operation there was no exchange of fire. Now, to your own knowledge, did any of the other groups, those groups led by Mr. Zinic or Mr. Balunovic or Mr. Drljo, did any of the other groups meet with resistance from the enemy and was there an exchange of fire, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: They did not find themselves in a situation where the extent of fire would have constituted a clash. What I heard was that there was sporadic shooting, and I don't recall. And I'm sure I didn't state that there was a clash, that a combat situation ensued where there was an exchange of fire of such an intensity that it would amount to a combat situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document P767, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina, I appreciate that you may not have seen this document, or perhaps you may be familiar. You see on the screen a report submitted by Mr. Celic on the events of the 26th August, and you can read the contents.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: On the 26th of August, 1995, at 0930 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: -- on the order --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You don't have to read it aloud. Can you read it for yourself. That's all right. It will be easier for you if you read it --

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we have - if the parties are not following the English document - the full Croatian version on the screen? It might be easier for the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let us know, Mr. Krajina, once you've finished.

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has not been able to read the whole of the document because it has not been on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Once you finish this page, Mr. Krajina, if you indicate, I will have the -- yes. Have you finished, Mr. Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No. Give me a moment. I have finished reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My first question is: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in this report, there is -- I'm drawing your attention to a particular section of this report, which records: "During the clearing of the terrain, both groups encountered resistance.
